plot_extraction.response_text:
Practical, self-serving Jane scorns romantic love, unlike her cousin Mattie, who remains devoted to the poor blacksmith’s assistant Jack Halibut. Mattie’s father forbids their courtship until Jack can support a wife, so Jack emigrates to America to make his fortune.

Three years later, Jack returns wealthy and secretly asks Mattie to meet him near the church. Jealous of Mattie’s opportunity, Jane follows her, locks her inside the church, and meets Jack herself. She falsely claims Mattie no longer loves him and implies that she, Jane, has remained faithful to him. Hurt and angry, Jack impulsively proposes to Jane, who accepts because of his wealth.

Jane forgets to release Mattie, who rings the church bell for help. Jack and several villagers arrive and find her trapped. Mattie joyfully embraces Jack, exposing Jane’s deception. Reunited, Jack and Mattie receive her father’s blessing and prepare to marry, while Jane is disgraced and loses her uncle’s trust, though she continues to insist that she acted for the best.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a comic first-person character narrative built around an unreliable, self-justifying voice. Jane tells the tale in a confidential, conversational manner, repeatedly appealing to the reader with phrases such as “I put it to you” and “if you’ll believe me.” She presents herself as practical, sensible and economically clear-sighted, but her own account steadily exposes her as jealous, calculating and dishonest. Much of the humour arises from this gap between her moral self-image and her plainly described behaviour. Even after locking Mattie in the church, fabricating a rejection and attempting to take Jack for herself, she insists that she acted “for the best.” The narration therefore delivers its judgement indirectly: Jane condemns herself without understanding that she is doing so.

The diction is colloquial, rural and historically marked. Non-standard grammar—“if they was,” “when the letter come,” “I says,” “leave me go,” “he don’t”—helps establish Jane’s social background and gives the prose the quality of spoken reminiscence. Idioms, clichés and proverbial expressions are frequent, including “put his foot down,” “all’s well that ends well,” “one wife is as good as another,” and “Satan to find some mischief still for idle hands to do.” Jane also relies on domestic and material comparisons: a face is “as long as a fiddle,” Jack frowns “like a July thunderstorm,” and she describes matching expressions to intentions as one might match ribbon to cloth. This figurative language is concrete rather than lyrical and reflects her practical, household-centred outlook.

The syntax imitates spontaneous speech. Sentences often proceed through long chains of clauses joined by “and,” “but,” “so” and “for,” with parenthetical qualifications, afterthoughts and comic corrections. Jane regularly weakens or revises incriminating statements—locking Mattie in was “a sort of joke,” “at least, I think so”—and such hesitations reveal motives she would rather conceal. Repetition gives the narration oral momentum, especially in constructions such as “and she… and she…” or “says I… says he.” Short sentences and abrupt exclamations punctuate moments of discovery or reversal, while rhetorical questions allow Jane to recruit the reader into her warped reasoning.

Dialogue occupies a large proportion of the story and is brisk, idiomatic and socially revealing. Speakers are differentiated less through elaborate description than through what they value and how directly they speak. Mattie’s language is emotionally simple and sincere; her father’s is paternal and proverbial; Jack’s becomes forceful and impatient under pressure; Jane’s is evasive, insinuating and strategically incomplete. She often avoids explicit lies at first, instead claiming to infer Mattie’s “mind” or withholding information until Jack supplies the conclusion she wants. This conversational manipulation is central to both the plot and the character comedy.

The structure is linear and anecdotal, beginning with Jane’s declaration that romantic love is nonsense and then furnishing a story that disproves her. Early exposition establishes the opposition between Mattie’s constancy and Jane’s materialism. Jack’s letter acts as the principal catalyst, and the narrative then accelerates through the secret meeting, Jane’s impersonation, the proposal and the forgotten imprisonment. Suspense is generated by practical objects and spatial arrangements: the church key, the prayer-book note, the ash copse, the locked door and the bell rope. The climax is theatrically visual and audible, with Mattie ringing the church bell until the community arrives. The final reconciliation is swift, while Jane’s exclusion from supper supplies a compact comic punishment.

Material detail is used as a form of characterization and moral contrast. Jane notices savings, prospects, bank deposits, dresses, bonnets, gloves, jewellery and Jack’s gold chain and diamond ring. Mattie, by contrast, scarcely registers Jack’s fortune and wears the old dress associated with their courtship rather than her fashionable new clothes. These details dramatize the difference between acquisitiveness and affection without requiring overt authorial commentary. Domestic work—jam-making, berry-picking, butter-selling and preparing tea—grounds the action in everyday rural life, while the church, farm, village and copse create a close communal setting in which secrecy is difficult to maintain.

The dominant tone is dryly comic, satirical and ironic rather than sentimental, even though the plot centres on faithful love. Jane dismisses Mattie as foolish, yet Mattie’s emotional directness repeatedly appears generous and perceptive beside Jane’s scheming. The story also uses comic disproportion: Jane treats attempted romantic theft as reasonable household management, describes deception as “acting for the best,” and responds to exposure by complaining that others cannot take a joke. Understatement sharpens the effect, especially in the closing lines, where “I had had all the supper I wanted” compresses humiliation, resentment and defeat into a seemingly practical observation.

The principal themes are love versus economic calculation, self-deception, envy, fidelity and moral blindness. The story initially appears to invite debate over whether marriage should be based on affection or financial security, but its deeper interest lies in the psychology of rationalization. Jane can interpret every event in a way that preserves her sense of virtue, while the reader sees that her supposed practicality masks covetousness. The ending does not reform her: she remains incapable of honest self-recognition. This unresolved blindness gives the conclusion its final ironic force and preserves the consistency of the narrative voice.

generation.response_text:
## Jane Acts for the Best

I never did hold with romantic love, and I do not now, in spite of what Uncle Peter and Mattie and half the village may say. Love is very well in songs, where nobody has to buy bacon or pay rent, and in story-books, where a young man’s coat never wears at the elbows unless he is a duke in disguise. But put love into a cottage with a smoky chimney, six shillings owing for flour, and twins expected before Michaelmas, and you will soon see what it is worth.

I put it to you: can kisses be boiled for broth? Will sighs mend a broken window? Does a girl’s heart keep her feet dry in November?

No. Yet because I have always possessed a little common sense, people call me hard.

My cousin Mattie was quite different. Mattie could look at a dead rose for twenty minutes and remember who had given it her. She kept bits of ribbon, old notes, and one cracked button in a box lined with blue paper, though none of them was worth a penny. When I told her so, she said they was precious to her.

“Precious!” says I. “That button come off Jack Halibut’s working waistcoat.”

“That is why,” says she.

And there you have Mattie all over.

We both lived with her father, my Uncle Peter Bell, at High Ash Farm. My own father and mother being dead, Uncle Peter had taken me in when I was twelve, and I worked for my keep from that day onward. I made no grievance of it. I skimmed the milk, fed the hens, helped with the cheeses, took butter into market, and could get more jam from a basket of gooseberries than Mattie could, because she was forever letting the pan boil over while she stared out of the window.

It was through one of these fits of staring that Jack Halibut first got a hold on her.

He was assistant to old Davy Crumb, the blacksmith, and he had strong shoulders, white teeth, and nothing else worth mentioning. He earned eighteen shillings a week when work was good, which it often wasn’t, and he had an old mother in a damp cottage beyond the mill. But Mattie said he had an honest face.

So has a cow, if you come to that.

Jack used to pass the farm of evenings, and Mattie would find business by the gate. If there was no business, she made some. She carried grain to hens that had gone to roost, fetched water when the pail was full, and once took a letter to the post that had no stamp and no address because, if you’ll believe me, it was a list of things she meant to buy in town.

I warned her.

“Mattie,” says I, “he may be handsome by candlelight, but candlelight don’t show holes in stockings.”

“He has no holes in his stockings,” says she.

“How do you know?”

She went as pink as boiled ham, which answered that question without answering it.

Uncle Peter found them by the orchard wall one Sunday after chapel. Jack was holding Mattie’s hand, or she was holding his; I won’t be unjust, though in my opinion the distinction is no larger than the difference between a sixpence and two threepences.

Uncle Peter put his foot down.

“You’re a good lad, Jack,” says he, “but a good lad without savings is a cart without wheels. It may be sound timber, but it won’t carry my daughter.”

“I can work,” says Jack.

“So can a horse,” says Uncle Peter, “and no sensible father marries his girl to one.”

Mattie began crying. She could cry as easy as another person sneezes.

Jack stood very straight and says, “What must I have before you’ll consent?”

“Enough to take a cottage, furnish it decent, and keep a wife through a bad winter.”

“Name the sum.”

Uncle Peter named two hundred pounds, which seemed to me generous, for I should have asked three. Jack’s face fell at first, as well it might, for he had then saved seven pounds, fourteen shillings, and a foreign coin that old Davy had taken for a farthing. But he looked at Mattie, and Mattie looked at him, and they went on looking till I began to feel like a stool left in the rain.

“I’ll get it,” says Jack.

“Not from Davy’s forge,” says Uncle Peter.

“Then I’ll go where I can.”

A month later he sailed for America.

Mattie made a great tragedy of it. She stood on the lane till the carrier’s cart was out of sight, and then she came indoors with her face as long as a fiddle and sat down beside the flour bin.

“Do get up,” says I. “You’ll mark your dress.”

“He is gone,” says she.

“That is generally what happens when a person goes.”

“He may never come back.”

“Then it is fortunate you did not marry him first.”

She looked at me as if I had said something cruel, when I was only pointing out the bright side. It is a curious thing that people who boast of tender hearts cannot bear plain truth.

Jack wrote from Liverpool, and then from New York, and then from a place called Pittsburgh, where there was iron works and smoke enough, by his account, to make our blacksmith’s chimney seem like a lady’s perfume bottle. His letters come regularly at first. Mattie read them until the folds split. She would not show them to me, which I considered unkind after all the times I had fetched them from the post.

I did see pieces, naturally. A letter left open on a kitchen table is no more private than a notice nailed to the church gate.

He wrote of long hours, hard labour, and wages four times what Davy paid. Later he had some share in a machine business, though what sort of machines Mattie could not explain. She only knew Jack was doing well and loved her. There might have been twenty pages about boilers and one line saying, “My own dear girl,” and that was the line she remembered.

For three years she waited.

Now, I do not deny that she had chances. Young Mr. Pottle, whose father kept the Red Lion and owned two cottages, asked her twice to walk out with him. Ned Swan, the miller’s nephew, brought her a china brooch from Birmingham. Even Mr. Rudge, a widower with a comfortable coal business and only four children, made inquiries.

I advised Mr. Rudge. Four children is a consideration, but so is a horse and trap.

“I love Jack,” says Mattie.

“You loved him three years ago,” says I. “That is not the same thing. A preserve may keep three years, but it won’t taste fresh.”

“He loves me too.”

“How do you know what a man is doing across the ocean? He may have married an American.”

“He would tell me.”

I laughed at that. Men do not always tell. If they did, where would lawyers get their dinner?

The truth was, though there is no use making too much of it, I had sometimes wondered about Jack myself. Not when he was poor, of course. A woman should never encourage a young man in habits he cannot afford. But as his letters spoke of contracts, partners, and money put away in a bank, he seemed to improve wonderfully.

It was not his fortune I cared for. I should like that understood. Money alone never attracted me. It was the steadiness that money represented, and the house it might furnish, and the servants it might pay, and the respect it might purchase. Any sensible girl would think the same.

When the important letter come, Mattie and I was making blackberry jam.

She had on a blue apron, and her hair was twisted up anyhow because of the heat. I was lifting jars from the boiler. The postman put the letter through the open window, and it fell beside the sugar scales.

Mattie knew Jack’s writing at once. Her hand shook so that she upset a saucer.

“You have broke the good one,” says I.

“He is coming home!”

She had not even opened the letter. That is the sort of foolishness I mean.

When she did open it, she read with both hands pressed to her cheeks. Then she laughed, then cried, then kissed the paper, which had travelled through several dirty post offices.

“Well?” says I.

“He is home already. He landed four days ago. He has been in London on business, and he comes here Thursday.”

“Does he?”

“He wants to see me before he sees Father. He says there is something he must tell me alone.”

I thought that sounded suspicious.

Mattie read on. Jack had arranged to meet her at eight on Thursday evening, by the old yew beside St. Bartholomew’s Church. He enclosed a little note meant to be put in her prayer-book, in case Uncle Peter should see the larger letter. There was no sense in that arrangement, for Uncle Peter never touched anybody’s prayer-book except in church, and then only his own, but lovers enjoy complication as cats enjoy string.

“What does he say of his circumstances?” I asked.

She looked blank. “He says he has succeeded beyond his hopes.”

“How far beyond?”

“I don’t know.”

“Does he mention figures?”

“No.”

“Property?”

“No.”

“Bank interest?”

“No, Jane.”

“Then what has filled three sheets?”

She held the letter against her breast. “Things you would not understand.”

That was gratitude for you.

On Thursday the house was in a flutter, though Uncle Peter knew nothing. Mattie changed her dress three times. First she put on the green muslin bought at Easter, then the grey with the pearl buttons, and then—what do you suppose?—she chose the old brown dress she had worn the day Jack left.

“It is faded at the shoulders,” says I.

“He liked it.”

“He liked you in it when you was eighteen and had a waist two inches smaller.”

She did not attend.

She put on no jewellery except the little brass locket Jack had given her, though she owned the china brooch from Ned Swan and a fine jet pin that had belonged to her mother. I offered to lend her my garnet earrings, but she refused.

“I want to look as I did when he went,” she says.

“You cannot. Three years has passed.”

“It has not changed how I feel.”

There are remarks so foolish that common sense has no tool to get a hold on them.

At half past seven Uncle Peter went to look at a sick calf in the far pasture. Mattie took her prayer-book, though it was not Sunday, and slipped from the kitchen.

I watched her from the window.

Now, I had not meant to follow. I had a batch of jam to cover, two pans to scour, and my best bonnet wanted new ribbon. But as the poet says, Satan finds some mischief still for idle hands to do, and I was not idle, so there was no reason Satan should be blamed. I followed because Mattie was innocent and impractical, Jack had been abroad among strangers, and somebody ought to see that all was proper.

Besides, I wanted to know how rich he was.

I kept far enough behind that Mattie did not hear me. She went down the lane, crossed the green, and entered the churchyard by the little side gate. The sun had gone behind the ridge, but the sky was still pale, and the church windows showed black under the ivy.

Jack was not yet there.

Mattie walked around the church twice, went beneath the yew, came out again, and then tried the church door. Old Mr. Page, the sexton, often left it unlocked when he had been sweeping, and that evening he had. Mattie went inside.

No doubt she wished to pray. Or perhaps she wished to look at herself in the brass tablet near the vestry, which gave a fair reflection if you stood sideways. I am not judging.

The key was in the outside of the lock.

I stood looking at it.

Then I looked toward the road.

Then, quite without forming any serious plan, I turned the key.

It was a sort of joke.

At least, I think so. Mattie had played jokes herself. Once she put salt in my tea, though she said it was an accident, and another time she hid my thimble. I only intended to keep her there a minute, so I might speak privately to Jack and discover his intentions. If his intentions was honourable, no harm would be done; and if they was not, Mattie would thank me.

There come a little knock from inside.

“Jane?” says Mattie.

I was surprised she knew it was me.

“Is that you, Jane?”

I made no answer. There is no use beginning an explanation before a person is calm enough to hear it.

Then I saw Jack coming up through the ash copse.

I knew him at once, though he was changed. He had grown broader and carried himself like a man accustomed to giving orders. His coat was dark blue and fitted him across the shoulders; his boots shone; there was a gold chain over his waistcoat, a diamond ring on his little finger, and a travelling bag in his hand that looked real leather, not pressed pasteboard.

You may say I noticed these things quickly. Some people notice sunsets. I notice what is useful.

He came straight toward me, then stopped.

“Jane Bell?”

“Jane Marsh,” says I. “But you are near enough.”

“Where is Mattie?”

No “How do you do?” No remark on my appearance, though I had put on a clean collar that afternoon. Travel may improve a man’s coat without improving his manners.

“Mattie?” says I.

“Yes, Mattie. She received my letter?”

“Oh, she received it.”

“Then why isn’t she here?”

I glanced toward the church. There was another knock, louder, but Jack took it for a branch tapping the door, or else he did not hear.

“Poor Jack,” says I.

His face altered.

“What do you mean?”

I had not decided what I meant, but once a conversation has started, it must be carried through, like washing on a windy day.

“I told her you would be disappointed,” says I.

“Told her? She isn’t coming?”

“She went out this evening,” says I, which was perfectly true. “But not to meet you.”

He frowned like a July thunderstorm. “Who did she go to meet?”

“I ought not say.”

“Jane, tell me.”

“You have been away a long time.”

“Three years, two months.”

“A girl can change in three years.”

“Mattie has written every month.”

“A woman may write from habit. I write down butter sales every Saturday, but that don’t mean I love butter.”

He took a step toward me. “Has she promised herself to somebody else?”

I lowered my eyes. I have always known how to make my face match an occasion, as one matches ribbon to cloth.

“You had better ask her.”

“I am asking you.”

“It is not for me to betray Mattie’s confidence.”

This was true too, because she had given me none.

He gripped the handle of his travelling bag. “Is it Pottle?”

I said nothing.

“Or Swan? I heard of that miller fellow.”

“I shall mention no names.”

“There is a man, then.”

“I did not say so.”

“You meant it.”

If a person insists on drawing conclusions, whose fault is that?

From inside the church came three sharp blows.

Jack looked round. “What is that?”

“Wood settling,” says I. “The church is old.”

He stared at the door, but then turned back. Hurt pride is a strong bridle.

“Why didn’t she tell me?” he says.

“She wished to spare you.”

“Spare me! By letting me travel four thousand miles?”

“Mattie never thinks of distances. You know how she is.”

He paced under the yew, and I could see anger and misery wrestling in him like two dogs in a sack. I felt sorry for him. I truly did. No woman likes to see a well-dressed man suffer.

“I made it,” says he. “I brought home more than Peter Bell asked. Ten times more. I own half the works now. I have bought the old Mercer house outside the village. I was going to tell her—”

“The Mercer house?” says I.

It had twelve rooms, a walled garden, stables, and a glasshouse, though three panes was cracked.

“Yes. I had it put in order. New carpets. A piano. She said once she wanted a room looking west.”

Mattie had said that when she was sixteen, after seeing a sunset. She had no practical use for a west room.

“She might have remembered,” says I.

He laughed, but there was no pleasure in it. “I remembered everything.”

That was when I began to perceive how deeply Mattie had wronged him—or would have wronged him, had what I implied been factual.

“You must not let it spoil your life,” says I gently.

“What do you care?”

“More than you know.”

He looked at me then. Properly looked, I mean. I had worn my plum-coloured dress, not from design but because the other was hanging to air, and my hair was smooth. I am not vain, but I knew I looked capable. Some men prefer a pretty fool, but a man who owns a machine business requires a wife who can reckon.

“You?” says he.

“There was more than one person who waited for news from America.”

I did not say I had waited for him. I had waited for the letters, which is different, but he was in no condition for fine distinctions.

“You never cared for me before.”

“A girl is not always free to show what she feels.”

Behind us, Mattie began rattling the latch.

Jack did not seem to hear. “You used to laugh at me.”

“I laughed to hide my tears.”

This come into my head from a song, and it served very well.

He walked away three paces, turned, and says, “If she has thrown me over, I will not crawl after her.”

“Naturally.”

“She shall see I can do without her.”

“Quite right.”

“One wife is as good as another, if she is faithful.”

I should not have put it so myself, but I understood his meaning.

He came close. His face was pale and set, and I knew he was acting from anger. But many a sound bargain is made because somebody is angry. If we waited for perfect temper, no pigs would ever be sold at market.

“Jane,” says he, “will you marry me?”

Now, some might say I ought to have asked for time. But delay can lose an opportunity, and I had long believed quick decisions to be the mark of a strong mind.

“Yes,” says I.

At that exact moment there came a thump from the church that made a pigeon fly out of the tower.

Jack glanced up.

“Those timbers want examining,” says I. “You being prosperous now, perhaps you could subscribe.”

He scarcely listened. “Then it is settled?”

“I do not go back on my word.”

Neither did Mattie, as it turned out, but there is no use looking ahead.

Jack took my hand. He did not kiss me, which I considered decent in a churchyard, though we was technically engaged. The diamond on his finger flashed. I wondered whether the ring was an American fashion or whether he might give it to me after having it made smaller.

“Your uncle will be astonished,” says he.

“He respects practical arrangements.”

“He’ll ask about Mattie.”

“She has made her choice, and we have made ours.”

Another bang come from inside. Then Mattie called my name, plain enough.

“Jane! Let me out!”

Jack’s hand dropped from mine.

“What was that?”

Before I could answer, the church bell gave one enormous clang.

Mattie had found the rope.

The sound struck over our heads and rolled across the green. A flock of rooks rose from the elm trees, Uncle Peter’s dogs began barking half a mile away, and old Mrs. Tapp came running from her cottage with a saucepan in her hand.

Clang!

Jack stared at the tower.

Clang! Clang!

“It appears,” says I, “that someone has been accidentally locked in.”

“Who?”

There are moments when no answer will improve a situation.

Jack seized the church-door handle and shook it. “It’s locked.”

“So it is.”

“The key’s here.”

He looked at the key, then at me.

I have never liked suspicious expressions.

“Open it,” says he.

“I was about to.”

“Open it!”

There was no need to shout. I turned the key.

By then people was hurrying from every direction. Mr. Page the sexton came puffing through the gate, followed by the baker, two boys, Mrs. Tapp with her saucepan, Ned Swan, and old Davy Crumb, who happened to be drinking at the Red Lion. Uncle Peter appeared last, running as fast as a man of sixty can run in boots clogged with pasture mud.

Jack pulled the door wide.

Mattie stood inside with the bell rope in both hands. Her old brown dress was dusty, her hair had fallen down, and there was a smear on her cheek where she had tried the little vestry window. She looked first at me, then at Jack.

“Jack!”

That was all she said.

She flew at him.

Not angrily. Not doubtful. Not like a girl who had changed her mind or promised herself to Mr. Pottle. She threw both arms around his neck before the whole village, and Jack dropped his travelling bag and held her as if she was the only living creature left after a flood.

It was excessively revealing.

“Mattie,” says he, “why was you in there?”

“She locked me in!”

Every face turned toward me.

“Do not make it sound worse than it was,” says I. “The key happened to turn.”

“You turned it,” says Mattie.

“I was keeping you from making a foolish secret meeting.”

“With Jack?”

“At the time I could not be certain who he was.”

“You called him Jack before he reached the gate,” says she.

It is surprising what people remember when they mean to be disagreeable.

Jack held Mattie by the shoulders and searched her face. “Jane told me you loved another man.”

“I did not,” says I quickly. “I let you infer it.”

Mattie’s eyes grew round. “Another man?”

“She said you had gone to meet him.”

“I said you had gone out, but not to meet Jack. You was inside the church, and he was outside, so strictly speaking—”

“Jane!” roared Uncle Peter.

He has always been impatient with exact language.

Jack’s face darkened. “You told me she had changed.”

“I said a girl can change. Everybody knows that.”

“You said she wrote from habit.”

“I offered butter sales as an example.”

“And you said you had waited faithful for me!”

“No. I said there was more than one person who waited for news from America. The whole village waited for news. Your mother waited. Davy waited. I waited. That makes considerably more than one.”

Mrs. Tapp gave a squeak and covered it with her saucepan. Several others began coughing. There was damp in the churchyard, but not enough to account for it.

Mattie still stared at Jack. “Did you believe her?”

“For five minutes,” says he miserably.

“What did you do?”

Here I thought Jack might show discretion. A gentleman should not repeat private words, especially words spoken under emotional strain.

But Jack says, “I asked Jane to marry me.”

Mattie let go of him.

The whole churchyard went silent.

Then Davy Crumb made a sound like a forge bellows bursting, and turned his back. The two boys sat down among the gravestones and stuffed their fists into their mouths. Even Uncle Peter’s eyebrows climbed.

“And I accepted,” says I, for if a fact must come out, it should at least come out accurately.

Mattie’s face went white.

Jack seized her hands. “I was hurt and furious. I thought you’d made a fool of me.”

“And so you asked Jane?”

“One wife is as good as another, he said,” I added, because I saw no reason I should carry all the blame.

Mattie pulled her hands away.

For one moment I thought my engagement might stand after all. A man cannot marry a woman who refuses to forgive him, and a promise is a promise.

Then Jack says, “No. That was a wicked, stupid thing to say, and if you never speak to me again, I’ll have earned it. But I crossed the ocean for you. I bought Mercer House for you. I remembered the west room. I’ve loved you every day, Mattie, even when I was too tired to eat. I believed Jane because I was afraid—afraid you had found someone better.”

“I could not,” says Mattie.

“Well,” says I, “you could, but you chose not to.”

Nobody attended.

Mattie began crying, naturally. Jack wiped the dusty smear from her cheek with his handkerchief. Then she touched his face as if she had to prove he was solid, and says, “I wore the brown dress.”

“I see that.”

“You always liked it.”

“I liked you in anything.”

That is the sort of remark men make before marriage.

Then they embraced again, and the villagers cheered, though what business it was of theirs I cannot say.

Uncle Peter came forward. “Have you got the two hundred pounds?”

Jack laughed. “I have two thousand and more, sir, besides my share in the works.”

“Then you have my blessing.”

“You said I needed enough to keep a wife through a bad winter.”

“With two thousand, you may keep her through several. Though,” Uncle Peter added, looking at Mattie’s dusty dress, “she never was expensive.”

I considered this unfair. Mattie might not care for expense, but she did not know how to prevent it. Only the week before, she had left cream where the cat could reach it.

“What about my engagement?” says I.

The cheering stopped.

Jack turned to me. “There is no engagement.”

“You asked. I accepted. There was witnesses near enough, if the church walls don’t count.”

“I asked under a false belief you created.”

“A belief is a belief.”

“You lied to me.”

“I did nothing of the kind. I was careful not to.”

“That makes it worse,” says Uncle Peter.

Now, I put it to you: how can avoiding a lie be worse than telling one? There is no satisfying some people.

Mattie came toward me. Her face was wet, and for a moment I thought she meant to strike me, though she had never struck anything larger than a moth.

“Why, Jane?”

I could have answered in several ways. I might have said I wished to test Jack’s constancy, which clearly needed testing. I might have said Mattie’s secret meeting was improper. I might have mentioned Mercer House, the bank money, the gold chain, or the west room, though those details would have been misunderstood.

So I says, “I acted for the best.”

“For whose best?” says she.

Some questions are mere traps.

Uncle Peter sent Mattie and Jack ahead to the farm, where he said they should have supper and discuss wedding dates. The villagers followed without invitation, because news travels best on its own feet. Mrs. Tapp went to fetch a pudding; the baker promised buns; Davy said there ought to be ale.

I started after them.

Uncle Peter blocked the gate.

“Not you.”

“I live at High Ash.”

“You may remain here till you have considered what you done.”

“I have considered it already.”

“That,” says he, “is what worries me.”

He took the church key from my hand and gave it to Mr. Page. Then he went off, leaving me among the graves while everybody else hurried toward lights, food, and celebration.

It was chilly by then. I sat on the low wall for a while and listened to the bell’s last trembling die away. Through the trees I could see Mercer House on the ridge, with sunset still caught in its upper windows. The west room, no doubt.

Mattie married Jack six weeks later.

I was not asked to be bridesmaid. Uncle Peter said he could not trust me near a church door. That was a poor joke, but everybody laughed.

Mattie wore white, though cream would have suited her colouring better, and Jack gave her a pearl necklace that must have cost thirty pounds. She scarcely looked at the pearls. She looked at him. Such waste is painful to witness.

They live at Mercer House now. Jack’s mother has the south cottage, warm and dry, and Uncle Peter goes to dinner every Sunday. Mattie has two maids, yet still makes Jack’s favourite blackberry jam herself, which proves that money cannot give a woman sense.

As for me, Uncle Peter did not turn me out, though he keeps the church key hung where I cannot reach it without a chair. He no longer lets me take the butter money to market, which is unjust, for I never stole a farthing. Jack speaks civil when we meet. Mattie has forgiven me, she says, but people who forgive you generally remember the matter at every convenient opportunity.

And what did I gain by it? Nothing. That ought to show I was not self-seeking.

They say all’s well that ends well. Mattie got Jack, Jack got Mattie, Uncle Peter got a rich son-in-law, and the village got enough talk to last through winter. Even Mr. Page got a new lock for the church, paid for by Jack.

Only I was excluded from supper that night.

But I had had all the supper I wanted.

## The Lighthouse That Remembered

The lighthouse stood three miles inland.

Travelers who noticed it from the railway usually assumed they had mistaken a church tower for something else. Those who asked about it in the village received no useful answer.

“The sea moved,” said the baker.

“The lighthouse moved,” said the postmistress.

“There was never a sea here,” said the schoolmaster, though the faded anchor tattooed across his wrist suggested that he was not always truthful.

Only old Mara Vale, who lived in a blue cottage at the edge of the wheat fields, offered an explanation longer than a sentence.

“The sea goes where it is remembered,” she said. “And so do lighthouses.”

People laughed when they repeated this, but never in front of her.

Mara had tended the lighthouse for forty-two years, despite the fact that no ship had passed beneath its beam in anyone’s living memory. Every evening she climbed the spiral stairs, polished the great brass lens, filled the oil reservoir, and lit the lamp. Its white beam swept across fields, barns, hedges, and the distant railway line. Cows looked up from their grazing as it passed. Foxes paused in the dark. Passengers in the midnight train sometimes woke to find light washing over their faces.

The villagers considered the ritual harmless. Mara was old, the tower belonged to no one, and the light had become as familiar as the moon.

Then one November morning, a letter arrived.

The postmistress herself delivered it, holding the envelope by its corner as though it had been fished from a drain.

“No stamp,” she said. “No postmark either.”

Mara took it without replying.

Her name was written on the front in pale blue ink. The paper smelled of salt.

Inside was a single sheet.

**Keeper,**

**The Bellweather will arrive on the night of the new moon. Keep the light burning.**

There was no signature.

Mara read the message twice. Then she looked east, beyond the bare orchards, toward the invisible horizon.

The new moon was three nights away.

That afternoon, she walked to the village shop and bought all the lamp oil it had.

“Expecting fog?” asked Mr. Pell, the shopkeeper.

“Traffic,” Mara replied.

By sunset, the story had spread from the shop to the tavern, from the tavern to the bakery, and from the bakery to every kitchen in the village. The Bellweather meant nothing to most people. To one man, however, it meant enough to make him drop a teacup.

Schoolmaster Orion Voss arrived at Mara’s cottage after dark. He was a tall, narrow man who dressed in black and carried himself with the stiff caution of someone balancing a glass of water on his head.

“Show me the letter,” he said.

Mara let him in.

Voss read it beside the stove. The color drained from his face.

“You know the name,” Mara said.

“No.”

“You have never been good at lying.”

“I teach geography. Lying is half the profession.”

He tried to smile, failed, and read the message again.

“The Bellweather disappeared fifty-six years ago,” he said at last. “It was a passenger ship. It sailed from Harrowport with one hundred and nine people aboard. A storm rose before midnight. No wreckage was ever found.”

Mara placed two cups on the table.

“And you were on it.”

Voss stared at her.

“Your tattoo,” she said. “The date beneath the anchor is the date it vanished.”

For a long moment, the only sound was the ticking of the stove.

“I was thirteen,” he said. “My father served as the ship’s physician. My mother and sister were passengers.”

“But you survived.”

“Yes.”

“How?”

Voss sat down slowly.

“I woke in a wheat field.”

Mara stopped pouring the tea.

“It was this field,” he continued. “East of the lighthouse. I remember the storm. I remember people shouting on deck. I remember my father tying a rope around my waist. Then I woke among green wheat under a clear sky. The lighthouse beam passed over me. I followed it here.”

“To this village?”

“There were only a few houses then. Your predecessor found me at the tower door.”

Mara had known the previous keeper, Elias Rook, only briefly. He had been nearly blind by the time she became his apprentice, yet he could identify every bird by its cry and every visitor by the rhythm of their footsteps.

“Elias never mentioned you,” she said.

“I asked him not to.”

“Did he tell you what happened?”

“He said the lighthouse shone on more than one kind of water.”

Mara looked at the blue writing once more.

Outside, the wind moved through the dry grass with a sound like a distant tide.

On the following day, clouds gathered over the village. They came from the east, low and dark, though the weather vane pointed west. By noon, rain had begun to fall, but the drops left white stains on windows and tasted of salt.

Children ran laughing through the streets with their mouths open. Their parents dragged them indoors.

At school, Voss dismissed his pupils early. He packed charts, notebooks, and a small brass compass into a leather case. Before leaving, he stood alone before the large map on his classroom wall.

The coastline was nearly two hundred miles away.

He touched Harrowport with one finger, then traced an imaginary path inland to the village.

That evening, he joined Mara at the lighthouse.

“You should stay home,” she said.

“So should you.”

“I work here.”

“You polish a lamp for ships that do not exist.”

“Tonight one might.”

They climbed together.

The lantern room smelled of oil, metal, and warm glass. Beyond the windows, the fields rolled into darkness. No stars were visible. The beam turned steadily, casting its circle over the land.

Voss opened his case. The compass needle spun without stopping.

“Useful instrument,” Mara observed.

“I find it honest in its confusion.”

Near midnight, a deep sound shook the glass.

A ship’s horn.

It came from somewhere beyond the eastern fields.

Mara tightened her hand around the railing. Voss closed his eyes.

Again the horn sounded, longer this time, filled with such grief that every dog in the village began to howl.

Lights appeared below as doors opened and villagers stepped into the streets. One by one, they came toward the tower carrying lanterns, shawls, umbrellas, and whatever courage they had managed to find.

The baker arrived first. “What was that?”

“Traffic,” Mara said.

Then the fog came.

It poured across the fields in silver walls, swallowing fences and trees. The lighthouse beam entered it and seemed to travel forever, a bright road leading into nothing.

The villagers crowded around the tower. Mara ordered them to stay outside, but no one listened. Soon the stairs were full of whispering people.

At one in the morning, the lamp flickered.

Mara checked the reservoir. It was full. She adjusted the wick, cleaned the burner, and inspected the gears. Everything was in order, yet the flame continued to weaken.

“The lens is cold,” Voss said.

A skin of frost crept across the glass.

“That is impossible,” Mara muttered.

“So is the horn.”

The light dimmed further.

Far out in the fog, a faint golden glow appeared.

It was not fixed like a window in a house. It rose and fell.

A ship’s lantern.

Then came another, and another, until a line of lights moved through the darkness where the eastern wheat fields should have been.

The villagers fell silent.

The fog thinned for a moment.

Black water covered the land.

It stretched from the base of the lighthouse to the horizon, lifting and lowering under a starless sky. Waves rolled over submerged hedges. The church spire rose from the water like the mast of a sunken ship. Rooftops stood as dark islands.

Yet the village itself remained dry. The people around the tower stared across an invisible boundary where grass ended and ocean began.

A great ship emerged from the fog.

The Bellweather was an old steam passenger vessel with two red funnels and a white upper deck. Rust streaked its hull. Seaweed hung from its rails. Its bow rose over the waves, turned slightly, and aimed toward the lighthouse.

“It’s coming too fast,” Mara said.

The beam had faded to a dull orange. The ship answered with another desperate blast of its horn.

Voss gripped the window frame. “It cannot see the reef.”

“There is no reef.”

“There was that night.”

He was thirteen again; Mara could see it in his face.

“Where?” she asked.

He pointed southeast. “A half mile out. We struck once, then turned broadside to the waves.”

Mara looked down. In that direction stood the oldest part of the village.

“The school,” she said.

Voss nodded.

Another tremor passed through the tower. The lamp went out.

Darkness fell with a force that seemed physical.

People cried out on the stairs. Below, lanterns swung wildly. From the sea came the grinding thunder of a vessel nearing rocks.

Mara struck a match. The flame burned blue, shrank, and vanished.

“The oil will not light,” she said.

Voss opened his case and pulled out a small book bound with string.

“What is that?”

“My journal. Everything I remember about the Bellweather.”

“This is not a time for reading.”

“It may be exactly the time.”

He tore out a page, rolled it tightly, and held it to the burner. Mara struck another match. This time the paper caught.

The flame was blue at first, then gold.

“What did you write there?” she asked.

“My sister’s name.”

The paper burned without blackening. Mara pushed it beneath the wick. The oil ignited, and light burst through the frozen lens.

Outside, the beam swept over the water.

The Bellweather’s bow turned.

Voss tore out another page. Then another. Memories written over half a century fed the lamp: the color of his mother’s traveling coat, the card games sailors played below deck, the taste of oranges in the dining room, the song his sister sang when thunder frightened her.

Each page made the beam brighter.

But the ship was still too far south. Its course would carry it through the schoolhouse reef.

“We need more light,” Mara said.

Voss looked at the few pages remaining. “This is all I have.”

Mara opened the lantern-room door.

“Bring paper!” she shouted down the stairs. “Letters, books, anything written by hand!”

The villagers obeyed with the speed of people who had finally been given a task they could understand. The baker offered old recipes. The postmistress brought undelivered letters. Mr. Pell sacrificed three years of account books after tearing out the pages that showed what Mara owed him.

They fed the paper into the flame.

The light grew, but not enough.

“These are only words,” Mara said. “They need memories.”

She seized the baker’s recipe for winter bread.

“Whose handwriting?”

“My mother’s,” he replied.

“Tell us about her.”

The baker looked embarrassed. Then the horn sounded again, and embarrassment ceased to matter.

“She sang while she kneaded dough,” he said. “Very badly. She knew only one verse of every song, so she made up the rest.”

The page ignited in Mara’s hands. The flame leaped twice as high.

Everyone understood.

The postmistress unfolded a letter. “This was written by a soldier who never came home. He asked me not to deliver it unless he did. I kept it forty years. He loved the miller’s daughter, but he was afraid to tell her.”

The letter burned white.

A farmer offered a page from his ledger. “This was the year my first son was born. I planted barley instead of wheat because I was too tired to remember which seed was in which sack.”

An old woman gave up a note written by her husband. “He left this under my pillow the morning after our wedding. It says, ‘You snore like a sawmill, and I love you anyway.’”

One by one, the villagers climbed to the lantern room with pieces of their lives.

The beam widened. It swept across the impossible ocean, brilliant as morning.

The Bellweather changed course. Its hull passed the submerged schoolhouse by a few yards.

People cheered.

Voss did not.

“It is still trapped,” he said. “Look.”

The ship had avoided the reef, but now it circled in the fog. Each time it approached the boundary near the tower, the waves pushed it back. Figures crowded its decks. They wore old-fashioned coats and life vests. Some raised their hands toward the light.

“They cannot reach shore,” Mara said.

“They did not reach it before,” Voss replied. “The night is repeating.”

“No. Not repeating.”

She watched the ship turn again. The dead—or the lost, if there was a difference—stood under the rain, waiting for the ending they remembered.

“The lighthouse brought you through,” she said. “Why only you?”

“I don’t know.”

“What happened just before you woke in the field?”

Voss pressed his fingers to his temples.

“My father tied the rope around me. My mother was holding my sister. There was a wave.” His voice shook. “The deck tilted. I fell against the rail. Someone grabbed me.”

“Who?”

“Elias.”

Mara stared at him.

“The old keeper?”

“He was on the deck,” Voss whispered. “But that makes no sense.”

Many truths sounded like nonsense when first spoken aloud. Mara had learned this from weather, machinery, and grief.

“Elias pulled you out,” she said. “Then he stayed here until I came.”

“As if the light requires a keeper.”

“Or a witness.”

The Bellweather sounded its horn once more.

On deck, a small figure slipped between the passengers and stepped toward the rail. Even across the distance, Voss recognized her.

His sister had been nine years old for fifty-six years.

“Clara,” he breathed.

The girl lifted a hand.

Voss turned toward the stairs.

Mara caught his arm. “Where are you going?”

“To the shore.”

“There is no shore.”

“There was enough of one for me.”

They descended through the crowd and emerged at the base of the tower. The black water began ten paces away. It rolled over wheat that appeared and disappeared beneath the waves.

The ship came closer, drawn by the light. Its engines beat like a slow heart.

Voss walked to the water’s edge.

Mara followed.

“You cannot bring them all through,” she said.

“I have to try.”

“No. You have to show them they may leave.”

He looked at her, not understanding.

Mara held up the final pages of his journal. Only one had writing on it.

“What is this memory?” she asked.

Voss looked down.

“It is the morning I woke here.”

“Read it.”

His voice was barely audible.

“‘I opened my eyes in a field under the turning light. The storm was gone. I called for my mother until I could not speak. A man carried me to the tower. He said I had crossed a great distance, and that those who loved me had sent me ahead.’”

The Bellweather drew near. The dead lined the rail.

Voss’s mother stood among them, one arm around Clara. His father stood behind her. None had aged.

They were close enough now that he could see rain on their faces.

His mother smiled.

Not the welcoming smile he had imagined all his life, but the brave, aching smile of someone saying farewell.

Voss sank to his knees.

“They sent me ahead,” he said.

Mara handed him the page.

He carried it to the water. A wave reached forward, touching the tips of his boots.

For a moment he seemed ready to step into the sea.

Instead, he folded the paper into a small boat.

He placed it on the water.

The paper boat did not sink. It sailed toward the Bellweather, shining brighter as it went. The lighthouse beam followed it across the waves.

When it touched the ship’s hull, dawn broke.

Golden light opened beneath the Bellweather, not above it. The sea became transparent. Far below, where darkness should have been, lay a sky filled with morning clouds.

The ship began to descend into that sky.

Its passengers waved. Some laughed. Some held one another. Clara climbed onto the lowest rail until her mother pulled her back.

Voss stood ankle-deep in the waves, weeping.

The Bellweather sounded its horn a final time. No grief remained in it.

Then the ship was gone.

The ocean withdrew with a sigh.

Water sank into wheat, roads, gardens, and stone. The church emerged dry. The rooftops settled under darkness. Fish flashed briefly in the grass and vanished before touching the ground.

All that remained was the smell of salt and the paper memories burning in the lamp.

The villagers stood silently until the real dawn appeared in the east.

In the weeks that followed, people disagreed about what they had seen. Some called it a miracle, others a shared dream. The baker insisted he had witnessed a ghost ship. The postmistress said the ship had been real and they were the ghosts. Mr. Pell submitted a request to the council for compensation for his lost account books.

Voss resigned from the school.

He did not leave the village. Instead, he moved into the blue cottage beside the lighthouse and became Mara’s apprentice, though he was older than she had been when Elias trained her.

“You may be disappointed,” she warned him. “Most nights, nothing happens.”

“Most nights are underrated.”

Together they repaired the lantern. The great lens had cracked during the cold, leaving a thin line through its center. No glassmaker could remove it, but when the lamp shone, the crack split the beam into two paths—one cast over the fields, and one angled strangely downward, as if illuminating deep water.

Years passed.

Mara’s knees grew weak, and Voss took over the evening climb. He kept the light burning through fog, snow, summer heat, and clear nights when it seemed foolish to guide anyone at all.

The village changed. Children grew up and moved away. New families arrived and asked why a lighthouse stood three miles inland.

“The sea moved,” said the baker’s daughter.

“The lighthouse moved,” said the new postmaster.

“There was never a sea here,” said a young teacher who wore no tattoos and believed only in approved textbooks.

Mara, sitting outside her cottage with a blanket over her legs, gave the answer she had always given.

“The sea goes where it is remembered.”

One spring evening, many years after the Bellweather came home, Voss climbed the tower and found a letter beside the lamp.

There was no stamp and no postmark. His name was written on the front in pale blue ink.

The paper smelled of pine trees.

Inside was a single sheet.

**Keeper,**

**The Northbound Express will arrive on the night of the first frost. Keep the light burning.**

Voss read it twice.

Then he looked from the window toward the abandoned railway line, where no train had run for thirty years.

Far away, beyond the dark fields, a whistle sounded.

Mara heard it from below.

She smiled, closed her eyes, and listened as the lighthouse began to remember something new.
